source: Aghazadeh, Ghasemi, Beyhaghi, Pishro-Nik (2026, v2) CGES: Confidence-Guided Early Stopping for Self-Consistency
finding: An independent group (not Aggarwal, Li or Lee, and not ConSol) re-ran Adaptive-Consistency (ASC), Early-Stopping SC (ESC) and Difficulty-Adaptive SC (DSC) as baselines with 10 seeds, next to its own Bayesian confidence stop rule. The ESC and ASC savings held at equal accuracy on easy sets. DSC saved the most calls but lost accuracy.
numbers: Budget B=16, 5 benchmarks (AIME24 30 items, GPQA-Diamond, MATH500, GSM8K, MMLU-Pro), two 7B open models, mean over 10 seeds. SC uses 16.0 calls. ESC and ASC variants average 8.6 to 9.1 calls (w=8 ESC 12.9) at -0.4pp. GSM8K: ESC/ASC 5.0 to 5.2 calls, CGES-LNS 2.41 calls at 94.1 vs SC 94.2. DSC about 5.2 calls avg but -1.9pp avg (AIME24 -3.0pp). CGES abstract: 16.0 to 6.7 calls (58%) within 0.4pp.
limits: Open 7B models only. Cost is call count, not tokens. CGES needs a per-answer confidence (token log-probs or a reward model). The CGES threshold shown is the smallest one within 0.2pp of SC on the same data, so it is tuned on test data. Table layout in the PDF text is garbled; row labels for ESC/ASC were matched by reading order.
agent_relevance: First re-run of the ASC and ESC savings by a different team (closes part of gap 6): they hold, about 40-45% fewer calls at B=16 with a 0.4pp loss. It does not test SPRT.

source: Aghazadeh et al. (2026) CGES, Appendix I: results at smaller budgets B=4 and B=8 (Tables 3 and 4)
finding: Against a small fixed budget the saving from agreement-style stopping is much smaller. At B=4 the ASC rule saved nothing (4.00 calls) and lost 0.5pp on average (GPQA -2.4pp). At B=8 ASC saved about 1 to 3.5 calls per item. DSC kept saving but its accuracy gap widened.
numbers: B=4 (10 seeds): SC avg 69.0% at 4 calls. ASC 68.5% at 4.00 calls. DSC about 2.3 calls, -2.7pp avg. CGES-LNS(arith) 69.0% at 2.94 calls avg (GSM8K 1.83, MATH500 2.58, AIME24 3.53, GPQA 4.00). B=8: GSM8K SC 93.9% at 8 calls, ASC 4.49 calls same accuracy, CGES-LNS 2.35 calls 94.0%; MATH500 ASC 5.41, CGES 3.17; AIME24 ASC 6.46, CGES 4.29 (76.3 vs 76.0); GPQA ASC 7.22 calls -1.9pp, CGES 7.67 -1.5pp; DSC -3.1pp avg at B=8. ESC omitted at B=4 and B=8 because its window of 4 is too large.
limits: Calls, not tokens. SC at B=4 and 8 is itself a majority of few draws, so ties matter. One group, open 7B models.
agent_relevance: Answers the first half of gap 1: the saving survives a budget of 8 on easy sets (about 40% on GSM8K and MATH500) but is zero at 4 for the plain posterior rule. Our cap should be 8 or more so the rule has room to stop.

source: Aghazadeh et al. (2026) CGES, Section 4.4: when the confidence signal is uninformative (GPQA)
finding: On GPQA-Diamond with the R1-Distill-Qwen-7B model every confidence signal, including a process reward model, separated correct from wrong answers only weakly. The posterior never concentrated, so the rule saved few calls and lost 1.5 to 2.4pp. The authors say no method that works only on the sampled candidates can recover an answer that was never sampled.
numbers: GPQA at B=16: SC 50.0%; CGES variants 46.4-47.9% at 11.5-14.2 calls; ESC(w=4) 48.0% at 12.88 calls. SC accuracy rose 44.9 (B=4), 47.9 (B=8), 50.0 (B=16).
limits: One hard multiple-choice set with a 7B model. The paper's guarantee needs a positive drift of the confidence signal toward the correct answer.
agent_relevance: On hard items with diffuse answers the stop rule rarely fires and the cap is reached. Treat 'rule never stops' as a hardness signal, not a failure (gaps 1 and 4).

source: Cordero-Encinar and Duncan (2025) Certified Self-Consistency: Statistical Guarantees and Test-Time Training
finding: Gives anytime-valid stopping for majority vote (Martingale Majority Certificate, using e-values). The certificate is about the model's own mode, not the truth. It assumes rollouts are conditionally independent given the prompt and that the mode is unique. At the error levels tried the certificate stops late and uses most of the budget.
numbers: Table 2 (Qwen2.5-Math-7B pre-trained): budget 10 -> about 9.7 samples used at alpha 0.1 and 9.4 at alpha 0.4; budget 50 -> about 39 and 38; budget 100 -> about 75 and 67. Accuracy equal to the full-budget vote (about 61.8-62.2% and 85.2-85.6% for the two settings). Test-time training lowers samples used further.
quote: violations (e.g., strong correlations or ties) weaken guarantees
limits: Single-turn reasoning benchmarks, small Qwen math models. Authors list correlated rollouts as future work. The guarantee is on Pr[mode estimate != true mode], so a confidently wrong mode is certified as consistent.
agent_relevance: Settles part of gaps 1b and 2: agreement-stopping, however rigorous, bounds error against the model's mode only. The error floor is P(mode wrong), which more sampling cannot lower. A rigorous certificate is conservative (saves 3 to 25% here), which explains why ConSol tuned alpha to extreme values.

source: Lee et al. (2025) ConSol: Sequential Probability Ratio Testing to Find Consistent LLM Reasoning Paths Efficiently (re-read for parameters)
finding: Re-read for gap 2. The paper says textbook SPRT uses p0 about 0.5 with p1 0.55 to 0.6 (its worked example uses likelihood ratios 1.2 and 0.8, i.e. p1 0.6). The reported results use p1 = 0.5001 and an extremely high type-I tolerance (alpha about 0.95), with the generation cap raised to 256. The authors say results depend on these sensitive settings and that a systematic calibration method is missing.
numbers: Tuned: p1=0.5001, alpha=0.949976 (SPRT); mixture SPRT Beta(1e6,1e6) prior, alpha=0.94994. Comparators: Adaptive-Consistency threshold 95%, p-value test alpha 0.05, SC capped at 40. Figure 3 sweeps the AC threshold over 0.74-0.9999 but the mSPRT alpha over only 0.94979-0.94997 (a window of 0.00018). Early stops happened before the 256 cap in all runs. Most top-two shares p1 were above 0.5 for o3-mini.
limits: The mSPRT alpha sweep is a narrow window around an extreme value, so accuracy sensitivity over a wide range of p1 and alpha is not reported. No seeds or intervals. Short-answer and multiple-choice tasks only. The text describes the parameters inconsistently (p1 0.6 in the example, 0.5001 in practice).
agent_relevance: Gap 2: there is no label-free recipe. The textbook p1 0.55-0.6 is not what produced the published savings. Do not copy ConSol's alpha: its Wald error guarantee is deliberately void (alpha about 0.95), so it acts as a tuned lead-margin heuristic. Set the threshold on a small labelled pilot or by simulating vote streams.

source: Chen, Davis, Hanin, Bailis, Stoica, Zaharia, Zou (2024) Are More LM Calls All You Need? Towards the Scaling Properties of Compound AI Systems
finding: Re-read for gap 5. The inverse U is a property of a mixture of easy and hard queries: more calls raise accuracy where the model's mode is right and lower it where the mode is wrong. All real-data runs use GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 only, averaged over 1,000 runs. On MMLU Physics the Vote split was 53% easy, 47% difficult.
numbers: Real data: GPT-3.5-turbo-0125, calls up to 100; four sets (MMLU Physics, TruthfulQA, GPQA, AVeriTeC). Synthetic two-level model: predicted optimal K matched the empirical optimal K in every row of Table 2. Optima were small (1, 2, 3, 4, 7 calls in the rows read; easy-share and success probabilities p1 0.4-0.5, p2 0.65-0.85).
limits: One 2024 model, no reasoning models, and no peak by difficulty bucket reported on real data. Theory says an inverse U needs the overall task to be easy (p1+p2>1) with a large hard share.
agent_relevance: The cap N should depend on the share of items where the mode is wrong, which needs labels. A cap of 8 to 16 is consistent with their optima and is cheap.

source: Cross-paper comparison: does majority vote keep rising with samples for recent open and frontier-class models? (CGES, DeepConf, Large Language Monkeys)
finding: No recent paper read shows an inverse U for reasoning models. The three that scale votes show gains that flatten. Evidence points to rise-then-plateau, not rise-then-fall, but none stratifies by difficulty.
numbers: CGES (7B models, 10 seeds): SC accuracy at B=4/8/16: AIME24 69.7/76.0/77.3; GPQA 44.9/47.9/50.0; MATH500 77.8/79.8/81.2; GSM8K 93.3/93.9/94.2; MMLU-Pro 59.4/61.0/62.1 (all rising). DeepConf Table 1 (512 traces): GPT-OSS-120B AIME25 pass@1 91.8 to Cons@512 97.0; Qwen3-32B HMMT25 51.9 to 63.3; DeepSeek-8B AIME25 76.9 to 82.3. Large Language Monkeys, Llama-3-8B-Instruct MATH: majority vote 40.50% to 41.41% from 100 to 10,000 samples (flat).
limits: Absence of a decline is not proof. Nobody plotted accuracy versus N for hard-only items on a frontier model. N ranges differ (up to 16, 512, 10,000).
agent_relevance: Gap 5 is mostly open but the risk looks lower than Chen et al. suggest. A cap near 16 is safe, and beyond that majority vote returns almost nothing.

source: Fu et al. (2025/2026) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf), re-read for gap 9 and a correction
finding: Correction: the mean token saving of 62.88% for DeepConf-low and 47.67% for DeepConf-high versus majority voting on DeepSeek-8B IS in the paper (text under Figure 7). Per-cell savings on GPT-OSS-120B at budget 512 run 32.0% to 84.7%. The implementation needs per-token top-k log-probs inside the inference engine (patched vLLM, logprobs=True, top_logprobs>=2).
numbers: Offline Table 1: GPT-OSS-120B AIME25 pass@1 91.8, Cons@512 97.0, Tail conf top-10% 99.9. Online (Table 2): GPT-OSS-120B AIME25 tokens 3.23e8 vs 0.49e8 for DeepConf-low (-84.7%, 97.1% to 97.9%); HMMT25 4.09e8 vs 0.97e8 (-76.2%). DeepSeek-8B AIME24: -77.9% tokens, accuracy 86.7 to 92.5. Qwen3-32B savings -43.8% to -66.8%.
limits: Open-weight models with exposed log-probs only. The authors state that models can be highly confident on wrong traces. Hosted reasoning APIs usually hide thinking-token log-probs (our inference, not in the paper).
agent_relevance: Gap 9: DeepConf is not usable through a hosted API without token log-probs. The 62.9% correction fixes the critique note. A verbalised score is the fallback (see d09).

source: Taubenfeld et al. (2025) Confidence Improves Self-Consistency in LLMs (CISC), re-read for gap 9
finding: Compared four ways to get a per-answer confidence for weighting votes. Verbalised scores are clearly worse than the model's own P(True) probability but still help.
numbers: Macro average over Gemma2, Qwen2.5 and Mistral models and MMLU, MATH, GSM8K, BBH. Cost reduction at budget 5 / 10: verbal binary 18% / 10%; verbal 0-100 22% / 30%; response probability 22% / 31%; P(True) 41% / 46% (plain SC needs 18.6 samples to match CISC at 10). Accuracy gain at budget 5 / 10: verbal binary 0.4 / 0.2; verbal 0-100 0.8 / 0.4; P(True) 1.6 / 1.1 points. Normalisation helps P(True) (32% to 46%) and verbal (20% to 30%).
limits: Weights votes, does not stop sampling. Open models only. P(True) needs probabilities and a second pass. Reasoning models not tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: verbalised 0-100 confidence recovers about two thirds of the token-probability saving at budget 10 (30% vs 46%). A hosted-API agent can use it and should expect 20-30%, calibrated per task.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Where an automatic verifier exists, coverage keeps rising with samples and success follows. Where only majority vote or a reward model is available, success plateaus near 100 samples while coverage keeps climbing.
numbers: Llama-3-8B-Instruct, MATH: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000. Majority vote and reward-model selection only 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range. SWE-bench Lite coverage rises from 15.9% to 56% at 250 samples (as cited earlier in this folder). Figure 8: many MATH/GSM8K items have a rarely sampled correct answer while the majority picks a wrong one.
limits: Llama-3 era models. The plateau is about picking the answer, not about stopping.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: when a checker exists, stop at the first pass. Agreement-stopping would cap us at the plateau. Agreement is the fallback for tasks with no check.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys, Section 4.2: imperfect verifiers
finding: Test-based verifiers are themselves imperfect, so stopping on 'tests pass' has its own false-stop and false-reject rate.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: 11.3% of problems have flaky test suites that sometimes fail even the gold patch. CodeContests: of 122 test problems with Python3 solutions, 35 have listed correct solutions that fail the provided tests (false negatives); some mutated test inputs break the problem's own rules.
limits: Specific benchmarks. False positives (wrong code that passes) are not quantified here.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: verify-then-stop beats agree-then-stop, but add a second weak signal (independent run or held-out test) when tests are thin. Agreement is useful as a tie-break among passing candidates, not as the stop signal.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated Errors in Large Language Models (ICML 2025)
finding: Across hundreds of models, errors are strongly correlated. When two models are both wrong they often give the same wrong option, and more accurate models are more correlated.
numbers: 349 LLMs on 12,032 multiple-choice questions (HuggingFace leaderboard), 71 LLMs on 14,042 (Helm), 20 LLMs on 1,800 resume pairs. On Helm, pairs agree about 60% of the time when both are wrong (random wrong choice would give 1/3). Same provider, base architecture or size raises agreement, and so does higher accuracy.
limits: Between-model agreement, not repeated samples from one model. Multiple choice only. It bounds but does not equal the false-stop rate of single-model self-consistency.
agent_relevance: Gap 1b: a shared wrong answer is the normal case, not an edge case. Do not count votes from different models as independent evidence, and same-model samples are even more tied. Require an independent check before trusting a unanimous stop.

source: Chen, Aksitov et al. (2023) Universal Self-Consistency for LLM Generation (Google)
finding: Agreement for free-form outputs can be defined by asking the model to pick the most consistent candidate among the samples. It works for summaries and open QA but gives no confidence or stopping rule, and more samples do not always help.
numbers: PaLM 2-L and gpt-3.5-turbo. TruthfulQA GPT-judge: PaLM 2-L greedy 62.1, USC 67.7; gpt-3.5 greedy 79.8, USC 82.5. GovReport ROUGE-1 38.8 greedy, 40.2 USC; SummScreen 30.6 greedy, 31.7 USC. USC did not improve SummScreen after 5 samples, GSM8K accuracy fell at 16 samples, and the authors call about 8 samples a sweet spot.
quote: universal self-consistency has not yet been developed to include the confidence estimation
limits: 2023 models, candidates bounded by context length, selection is one LLM call. No stop rule tested.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the agreement measure for open-ended text is a model-judged 'most consistent' pick, which gives no vote share. A stop rule needs a pairwise same/different judgement per sample. No paper found tests that.

source: Yao, Shinn, Razavi, Narasimhan (2024) tau-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction
finding: For multi-step agent tasks, 'same answer' can be defined as the same final database state. Under that measure repeated runs of one agent disagree a lot.
numbers: Success is judged by comparing the final database state with a goal state. Best function-calling gpt-4o agent: under 50% task success (pass^1), and pass^8 below 25% in the retail domain.
limits: 2024 models. The paper measures consistency, not a stopping rule.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: for agent tasks the usable agreement measure is equality of the outcome state. Agreement between runs is low enough that 'stop when runs agree' would fire rarely. Run-to-run disagreement is information: escalate, do not average.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Make Every Penny Count: Difficulty-Adaptive Self-Consistency (DSC), re-read for gap 4
finding: The difficulty probe is a model-ranked batch order, only moderately correlated with human difficulty labels. The paper reports no error rate on the items where one CoT sample and SC disagree, only the disagreement share.
numbers: CoT vs 40-sample SC disagree on GSM8K for 15.2% of items (GPT-3.5) and 3.8% (GPT-4). Difficulty ranking vs human labels on MATH subsets: GPT-4 Spearman 0.624, Pearson 0.627, Kendall 0.491; GPT-3.5 Spearman 0.440. Geometry weakest (Spearman 0.540 GPT-4, 0.415 GPT-3.5). The independent CGES test found DSC at -1.9pp avg at B=16, -2.7pp at B=4, -3.1pp at B=8.
limits: Ranking is relative within a batch, with a pre-sample size of 4. It is not an agreement probe on the single item.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open: no source gives the miss rate of a one-sample probe on the hard items. The independent CGES test shows DSC's gate costs 2 to 3 points, so use a probe only after measuring its miss rate on our tasks.

source: Feng, Alonso, Odonnat, Feofanov, Redko (2026) Optimal Self-Consistency for Efficient Reasoning with LLMs (Blend-ASC)
finding: Another independent group tested Adaptive SC (the posterior-threshold stop) against fixed allocation. Its advantage shrank at the larger budget and it failed to reach the SC target for one model and set. Their hyperparameter-free allocation beat it.
numbers: Average sample-efficiency gain to match SC@64: fixed allocation 4.09x, Adaptive SC 4.36x, Blend-ASC 5.33x. To match SC@128: fixed 3.40x, Adaptive SC 2.13x (worse than fixed; 128 samples used for Llama-3.2-3B on GSM8K without reaching the target), Blend-ASC 4.29x. Models Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Qwen2.5-32B; temperatures 0.4-1.0. Blend-ASC takes 1.8 s on GPQA-Diamond at budget 128.
limits: Metric is 'reducible error' against the model's limiting mode, not the true answer. It allocates across a batch, so needs the whole question set in hand. Preprint. No SPRT baseline.
agent_relevance: Gap 6, partial: the posterior stop rule is threshold-fragile when the target is high, a second independent report that its savings are not uniform. SPRT itself still has no independent test.

source: Hu, Tan, Wang, Qu, Chen (2025) Multi-Agent Debate for LLM Judges with Adaptive Stability Detection
finding: For debate, a different signal replaces vote share: the count of correct judges per round (out of 7), fitted as a Beta-Binomial mixture, with a Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance between rounds below 0.05. It stops after 2 to 8 rounds of a 10-round maximum at almost no accuracy loss. Debate helped on hard judgment sets and hurt on some easy ones.
numbers: Ensemble 7, max 10 rounds, KS threshold 0.05. Accuracy change versus full 10 rounds from -1.03 to 0.0 points (Qwen-2.5-7B BIG-Bench 5 rounds 70.07, -0.20; JudgeBench 5 rounds 56.54, -0.16; LLMBar 4 rounds 81.70, -0.67). Table 1: Llama-3.1-8B BIG-Bench single 74.37, majority 76.60, debate 72.20; JudgeBench single 58.32, majority 59.52, debate 59.68.
limits: The mixture is fitted on counts of correct judges, which needs labels at fit time. Small open models. No equal-cost comparison with a plain 7-vote majority.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a stability test on the whole judge distribution is a workable signal, but it stops on 'no further change', which is not the same as correct. Pair it with Morandi's calibration check (d18).

source: Morandi (2026) Sequential Consensus for Multi-Agent LLM Debates: A Wald-SPRT compute governor (re-read for gaps 8 and 10)
finding: Pre-flight check: fit the judge's consensus-score distribution under 'consensus' and 'no consensus' and compute the KL between them. If KL is near zero the SPRT cannot separate and runs to the cap. The paper also simulates SPRT under correlated scores. The headline savings are not significant (confirmed).
numbers: GSM8K KL(f1||f0)=9.80, KL(f0||f1)=2.61, 98% stop in round 1, 1.01 rounds, 4.06 calls, 97.0% vs fixed-5 99.0% at 15 calls. MMLU KL about 0 (n=40 calibration), 99.5% of items hit cap 8, 32.0 calls (2.1x fixed-5), 94.2% vs 3-call majority 94.4% and fixed-5 93.8%. Wald 95% CI about +-4.4pp at n 191-200; no pairwise difference significant. AR(1)-correlated score simulation, nominal alpha=beta=0.05, 50,000 trajectories: rho=0 gives (0.015, 0.017); rho=0.2 (0.026, 0.029); rho=0.41 (0.044, 0.048); rho=0.6 (0.065, 0.072); mean rounds 2.38 to 2.69.
limits: Simulation, not a proof. Judges were gpt-5, claude-opus-4-6 and gemini-2.5-pro on 200 items per task. The authors list adversarial debates as untested.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: run the KL check before trusting any convergence signal. Gap 10, partly: Wald-style error rates degrade gracefully, about 1.5x nominal at lag-1 correlation 0.6 in this simulation. The below-nominal rates at rho=0 show Wald's bounds are conservative.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Adaptive-Consistency: threshold sweep and stated limitation (re-read)
finding: The 95% confidence threshold is a hand-set constant used on all data sets. The paper sweeps the threshold from 0.5 to 1 (Figure 2) and compares to SC at equal average cost (Section 5.2). The authors list stopping-criterion sensitivity as a limitation: the majority can look stable and still be wrong.
numbers: Threshold swept 0.5-1.0, default 0.95. Stop-check compute time: Beta 0.03 ms vs Dirichlet about 101 ms and CRP about 95 ms (Table 2).
limits: The original authors' own sweep. No seeds reported in the parts read.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: even the original posterior rule uses an unlabelled constant. A conservative 0.95 with a cap of about 16 is the standard. No paper gives a no-label method for tuning it.

source: Wald (1945) Sequential Tests of Statistical Hypotheses; Wald and Wolfowitz (1948) Optimum Character of the Sequential Probability Ratio Test (attempted)
finding: Not opened: the publisher returned a bot-check page instead of the PDF, and I did not work around it. The statement that SPRT minimises expected sample size among tests with the same two error bounds, for i.i.d. observations and two simple hypotheses, still rests on secondary sources. The 'about half the samples' figure remains unverified.
numbers: none verified
limits: The theorem is for independent, identically distributed observations and simple hypotheses. Nothing opened this session covers dependent votes.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open on the primary proof. Practical stand-ins: Morandi's simulation (d18) and the i.i.d. assumption flagged by Certified SC (d04).

source: Pointer for dependent data: Lai (1998) IEEE Trans. Information Theory 44; Tartakovsky (1998) Statistical Inference for Stochastic Processes 1 (not opened)
finding: Recalled from memory, not read: asymptotic optimality of SPRT-type tests for non-i.i.d. data holds when the log-likelihood ratio converges at a suitable rate, and sample-size optimality holds only in the limit of small error. Listed as the next sources to open.
numbers: none
limits: Unverified. Citation details are from memory.
agent_relevance: For correlated samples, expect sample-size optimality to hold only asymptotically and only for the model-implied likelihood, not a mis-specified one.
